Plow
PLOU
v. and n.
From Saxon ploh; the Authorized Version prints both plow and plough. Webster 1828: to turn up, break, or till the ground with a plough. Scripture uses it of diligence, of the sluggard, of sowing wickedness, and of the man who looks back.

Biblical Definition

Plow in Scripture is the labour that must be done before anything can grow, and it is used to test a man in four ways. Proverbs tests his diligence: The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing (Proverbs 20:4) — the cold is real, the excuse is reasonable, and the harvest is empty. Hosea tests his moral sowing: Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity; ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men (Hosea 10:13). Wickedness is not merely committed but cultivated, and the crop comes up. Paul tests the churches’ obligation to their ministers, applying the ox-and-corn law of Deuteronomy: he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope (1 Corinthians 9:10). And the Lord tests a would-be disciple’s attachment to what he is leaving: No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62) — spoken to a man who asked only to go home and say farewell.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PLOW (also written PLOUGH) as to turn up, break, or till the ground with a plough; and figuratively, to furrow, to run through, or to labour with painful effort.

expand to see more

PLOW, v.t. — To turn up, break, or till the ground with a plough, for the purpose of sowing.

To furrow; to make furrows or ridges in; to divide, as a ship ploughs the sea.

PLOW, n. — An instrument for turning up and preparing the soil for the reception of seed.

Figuratively, to labour with painful effort, or to prepare the way for what is to follow.

From Saxon ploh; the Authorized Version prints both plow and plough in different places.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 20:4 — "The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold; therefore shall he beg in harvest, and have nothing."

Hosea 10:13 — "Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity; ye have eaten the fruit of lies: because thou didst trust in thy way, in the multitude of thy mighty men."

1 Corinthians 9:10 — "Or saith he it altogether for our sakes? For our sakes, no doubt, this is written: that he that ploweth should plow in hope; and that he that thresheth in hope should be partaker of his hope."

Luke 9:62 — "And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God."

Modern Corruption

Luke 9:62 is spoken to a man whose request — to say farewell to his household — was entirely reasonable, and the Lord’s refusal to soften it stands against a discipleship offered on terms the hearer sets.

expand to see more

Three men come to Christ in the last verses of Luke 9 and none of them is handled the way modern practice would handle them. The first volunteers to follow anywhere and is told the Son of man has nowhere to lay His head. The second is called and asks first to bury his father. The third asks only to bid farewell to those at home — the very thing Elisha was permitted when Elijah cast his mantle on him — and receives the plough saying. The Lord is not indifferent to family; He commanded honour to parents and provided for His mother from the cross. He is refusing to let the call be renegotiated after it has been given. Ploughing with the head turned produces a crooked furrow, and a discipleship that keeps looking back at what it left will produce nothing straight.

Hosea 10:13 supplies the agricultural principle underneath, and it is the one modern moral thinking most consistently denies. Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity. Sin is not merely an act with consequences attached from outside; it is a sowing, and it grows a crop of its own kind. Paul states it flatly: Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap (Galatians 6:7). Proverbs 20:4 shows the same law in the ordinary business of a farm, and it is a mercy that it does: the man who will not work in the cold begs in the harvest, and no one has to explain the connection to him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew charash (H2790), to plow, to engrave, and also to be silent; machareshah (H4281), a plowshare; Greek arotriao (G722), to plow; arotron (G723), a plough.

expand to see more

Hebrew charash (H2790) — to cut in, to plow, to engrave; the same root means to devise, as one who deviseth mischief.

Hebrew machareshah (H4281) — a plowshare; they shall beat their swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4).

Greek arotriao (G722) — to plow; he that ploweth should plow in hope (1 Corinthians 9:10).

Greek arotron (G723) — a plough; only at Luke 9:62.

Hebrew nir (H5215) — tilled ground, a fallow field; Break up your fallow ground (Hosea 10:12).

Usage

"The sluggard will not plow by reason of the cold (Proverbs 20:4) — a real cold, a reasonable excuse, and an empty harvest."

"Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity (Hosea 10:13) — sin cultivated, and the crop coming up."

"Having put his hand to the plough, and looking back (Luke 9:62) — a call that may not be renegotiated."
